You use the gerund for simultaneous actions, manner, cause and condition (camminando, sbagliando s'impara, pur essendo stanco) and review relative pronouns, the conditional and the trapassato.
Walking along the Arno, I was thinking of you.
Although he was tired, he came out with us.
Having finished work, we went to dinner.
To form the gerund: -ando, -endo; irregular: facendo, dicendo, bevendo.
To use the gerund for two simultaneous actions: Cucinando, ascolto la radio.
To express manner, cause or condition with the gerund: Studiando, imparerai.
To recognise the past gerund: avendo finito, essendo arrivato.
To review the unit: relatives, the conditional, the trapassato.
Mid-December. Matei walks into the trattoria kitchen and closes the door. Graziella and Pietro look at him curiously.
Graziella, Pietro, I have to tell you something. But it's a secret.
A secret! I can keep secrets. I kept Dad's for three months!
(takes out a little box) This is my grandmother's ring. She gave it to me in August, saying: "For the girl in the green dress."
Oh, Matei! You want to ask Giulia to marry you?
Yes. On Christmas Eve, before leaving for Sibiu. But I don't know how to do it. Just thinking about it, I tremble.
Aldo asked me while we were walking across the Ponte Santa Trinita. No ring, no flowers. Just with his heart.
I'd do it on one knee, like in films! And then I'd have a brass band play!
A brass band? Pietro, knowing Giulia, she'd run away.
Keep it simple. Bring her to dinner here, then walk her home over the bridge. You'll know the rest at the right moment.
And what if she said no?
Matei, that girl has been on time for nine months. Even though she's Neapolitan! Trust me: she'll say yes.
And me? What do I do?
You do the hardest thing: keep quiet until the twenty-fourth.
"chiedere la mano" = to ask someone to marry you
The gerund is stressed on "AN" / "EN": cam-mi-NAN-do, cre-DEN-do, dor-MEN-do.
The gerund never changes (neither gender nor number) — just like in Romanian.
Pronouns are attached to the end: pensandoci (thinking about it), dicendolo (saying it), guardandola (looking at her).
While walking, I was thinking of you.
Essendo stanco, sono rimasto a casa.
Being tired, I stayed at home.
By studying every day, you'll learn.
The subject of the gerund must be the same as that of the main verb! "Camminando, mi è caduto il telefono" is wrong (the phone wasn't walking). Correct: "Mentre camminavo, mi è caduto il telefono."
Although she lives in Florence, she's never been to the Uffizi.
Even if I wanted to, I can't come.
It's an elegant alternative to "anche se" (even if) or "benché" (although), which takes the subjunctive.
AVENDO / ESSENDO + participle = an action completed BEFORE the main one:
Having finished work, we went to dinner.
Having arrived late, she didn't find a seat.
With ESSENDO the participle agrees: essendo arrivata, essendo partiti.
La città in cui sono nato. Chi dorme non piglia pesci.
Quando sono arrivato, era già partito.
Camminando sotto la neve, le ha chiesto la mano.
With these you can tell complex memories and make plans: that's what a solid A2 means.

It almost never snows in Florence. Graziella always said so, the guidebooks said so, even the weather forecast said so. But on the 24th of December, at about six in the evening, coming out of the trattoria, Matei saw the first flakes falling.

The dinner had been perfect. Graziella had cooked for twelve people, even though there were only six of them. Pietro had kept the secret for ten whole days, going redder every time he looked at Giulia. Marco and Sara, Florentines for two months now, had brought the panettone.

Professor Bellini had also dropped in for a glass of wine. He had brought Matei the tickets for Sibiu and, looking at Giulia, had said only: "Please, Matei. Don't keep anyone waiting." Nobody had understood, except Graziella, who had smiled without a word.
At about ten, Matei stood up. "I'll walk Giulia home," he said, trying to sound normal. Graziella squeezed his arm as she passed. Pietro pretended to look at the ceiling, whistling.

Outside it really was snowing. The snow was falling slowly on via Maggio, on the roofs, on the parked bicycles. Walking towards the river, Giulia laughed like a child, trying to catch the flakes on her tongue. "I've never seen it like this in Naples!" she kept saying.

Matei, on the other hand, didn't speak. He kept his right hand in his pocket, gripping the little box so hard that his fingers hurt. He was thinking about everything that had happened in fifteen months: the first day at the workshop, the stained shirt, the bay in the frame, the Bridge of Lies, Ernesto Bellini's letter.

They reached the Ponte Santa Trinita. The river was black and silent, and over the Ponte Vecchio the yellow lights seemed to float in the snow. There was nobody about. Only the two of them and the white city.
Matei stopped. "Giulia," he said. She turned, with snow in her black hair. He had prepared a whole speech and rehearsed it for days in front of the mirror. But at that moment he forgot all of it.

So he did what Graziella had said: he spoke from the heart. "My grandmother gave me this ring saying it was for the girl in the green dress. I drew her when I was ten, without knowing who she was. Now I know." He took out the little box, trembling. He didn't kneel: the snow was too wet and he was too emotional. "Will you marry me?"

Giulia looked at him for a long moment. Then she laughed and cried at the same time. "Matei, you really are slow. I told you back in March." She took his face in her cold hands. "Yes. Yes, I'll marry you. But only if your mother teaches me sarmale in Sibiu."
He put the ring on her finger. It fitted perfectly, as if it had been made for her. They stood there, holding each other, while the snow covered the bridge, the river, the city.

On the other side of the river, behind a window on via Maggio, three figures were watching them through opera glasses: a grandmother, a nine-year-old boy and a very fat cat. "She said yes!" Pietro shouted. "I told you so," Graziella replied, wiping her eyes. And Michelangelo, who understood nothing, meowed anyway.
